extracted.intended_audience: activity comptrollers, contracting officers, and other federal acquisition/procurement personnel (examples: Navy comptrollers and program analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and decision criteria for applying OMB Circular A-76 to evaluate whether government activities should be performed in-house or contracted out, including the A-76 process steps, decision checklists, contract types, and thresholds for award/return to government performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole source contracting statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Competition in Contracting Act, there are seven statutory exceptions which allow for sole source contracting: (1) Only one responsible source; (2) Unusual or compelling urgency; (3) Industrial mobilization purposes; (4) Based on an international agreement or Foreign Military Sales requirement; (5) To meet a statutory requirement; (6) In the interest of national security; (7) In the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contracts must be formally justified and receive an appropriate level of approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special contracting methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Special contracting methods include multi-year contracting, options, and leader company contracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General purpose is to increase economic efficiency; each method has specific limitations, objectives and requirements that must be considered when selecting contracting method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when negotiating contract type
rubrics_metrics.description: Key factors to take into account when negotiating the type of contract: (1) Price competition; (2) Cost analysis; (3) Price analysis; (4) Urgency of requirement; (5) Type and complexity of the requirement; (6) Adequacy of contractor's accounting system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiation of contract price and type are tightly linked; efforts must provide reasonable risk and sufficient incentive for contractor to perform economically and efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract type categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract types vary according to the degree and timing of responsibility assumed for costs by the contractor and the amount and nature of the profit incentive; generally divided into Fixed-Price contracts and Cost-Reimbursement contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection requires negotiation and sound judgment by the Contracting Officer; choice affects risk allocation and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm Fixed Price Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Government and contractor agree to a fixed price for goods or services which is not subject to adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places maximum risk on contractor who assumes responsibility for cost control and any loss or profit; provides maximum incentive for contractor to control costs. [Ref. 3:p.16-2]

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Redeterminable Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Used when uncertainties preclude a firm fixed-price contract; provides a firm fixed price for an initial period and prospective redetermination at a specified time for subsequent periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires contractor to have acceptable cost accounting system capable of accurately capturing and reporting costs to be used for subsequent redeterminations of price. [Ref. 3:p.16-4]

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Incentive Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractor and Government agree on target costs and a pricing agreement to incentivize contractor to reduce costs and earn additional profit if under target costs; a negotiated price ceiling is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor shares savings according to a predetermined formula; cost overruns reduce profit; can be firm target or successive targets depending on cost/profit targets. [Ref. 3:p.16-4]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Incentive-Fee Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies a target cost, target profit, minimum and maximum fees and a fee adjustment formula; fee is adjusted based on relationship between allowable costs and target costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to fixed-price incentive but without a price ceiling; normally used for test and development contracts; encourages cost control on high-risk projects. [Ref. 3:p.16-10]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Fee-Award Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A cost-reimbursement contract that provides a base fixed fee plus an award amount based on excellence in quality, timeliness, technical ingenuity, and cost-effective management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows Government flexibility by realigning weights in the award fee formula each award period; used to emphasize particular contractor performance attributes. [Ref. 3:p.16-10]

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides contractor a fixed fee in addition to reimbursement for allowable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually utilized where great risks and uncertainties exist, such as research and development work. [Ref. 3:p.16]

rubrics_metrics.name: Other contract forms and appropriate uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Other contracts/agreements include indefinite quantity contracts, definite quantity contracts, requirements contracts, time and materials contracts, labor hour contracts, letter contracts, basic ordering agreements, and blanket purchase agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each has particular uses (e.g., unknown exact quantities or delivery times, small purchases, repetitive procurement of services/goods); government needs to evaluate needs and contractor abilities before choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting process components
rubrics_metrics.description: The contracting process consists of six basic components: (1) Planning; (2) Source solicitation; (3) Source evaluation and selection; (4) Negotiation; (5) Award; (6) Contract administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process duration depends on cost, contracting method, and item/service; each component has specific tasks and required documentation. [Ref. 2:p.4; 2:p.7; 2:p.9; 2:p.10; 2:p.1]

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning phase requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning includes determination of procurement method, development of acquisition strategy, determination of contract type, development of solicitation document, evaluation of specifications for bidding, circulation of draft requests for proposals, and determination of data necessary for negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning sets the foundation for solicitation and negotiation; reference: [Ref. 2:p.4].

rubrics_metrics.name: Source solicitation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Source solicitation phase releases solicitation documents, applies modifications/changes, and may include bidder's conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicitation documents must include specific requirements when contracting out for commercial activity (see PWS and solicitation stipulations). [Ref. 2:p.4]

rubrics_metrics.name: Source evaluation and selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation involves assessing bids/offers to determine the lowest responsive and responsible bidder/offeror, establishing competitive range, applying source selection criteria, and preparing for negotiations using cost and price analysis and contractor data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to use both cost and price analysis and relevant contractor data to determine responsibility and responsiveness. [Ref. 2:p.7]

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation phase scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiation includes negotiating delivery schedule, costs, pricing structure, profit or fee, and technical aspects of the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not applicable to sealed bid method; key component in negotiated procurements. [Ref. 2:p.9]

rubrics_metrics.name: Award phase tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Award involves final agreement on contract terms and conditions, contract preparation, legal review, signatures, and publicizing the award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all required approvals and reviews are completed prior to award. [Ref. 2:p.10]

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract administration involves Government monitoring of contractor performance including production surveillance, quality assurance, cost auditing, termination settlements, property management and contract payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active oversight is required to ensure contractor meets PWS and performance standards. [Ref. 2:p.1]

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-76 policy is based on three principles: (1) Achieve economy and enhance productivity by comparing contracting vs in-house costs; (2) Retain inherently governmental functions in-house; (3) Rely on commercially available sources for commercial products and services when more economical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles guide decision-making on whether to contract out or retain services. [Ref. 6:p.2]

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated agency coordination and milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must designate a department to coordinate and monitor commercial activity milestones, establish reporting milestones, task activities for internal review, maintain a commercial activities inventory, and monitor progress toward competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: OPNAV 43 coordinates Navy commercial activity programs; agencies should ensure responsibilities and reporting are assigned. [Ref. 8:p.J-13]

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Work (SOW) / Performance Work Statement (PWS) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in the study is to analyze the task to identify its function and create a Statement of Work which becomes the Performance Work Statement (PWS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PWS is the basis for Government and commercial cost estimates and for the solicitation document; its accuracy and scope must be flawless to obtain true equal-work cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Assurance Plan requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent with the SOW/PWS, design a Quality Assurance plan for a possible commercial service contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to provide the Government a course of action to ensure the activity is performed properly by the commercial source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish Most Efficient Organization (MEO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct an in-depth organizational and staffing analysis leading to establishment of a Most Efficient Organization (MEO) which can perform the mission efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO is used to develop the in-house cost baseline for comparisons; may cause staffing decreases or, in some cases, expansion to conform to MEO. [Ref. 7:p.40]

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation stipulations for commercial activity competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicitation package must notify contractors that award is based solely on cost comparison between commercial bidders and the government's MEO estimate, and that the solicitation may be canceled if government cost is lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor must also be informed they are required to offer employment to any qualified government employee displaced by the commercial activity study. [Ref. 7:p.41]

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract award cost threshold (contractor must be ≥10% less)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of bids, contractor bids are compared with MEO costs; commercial proposals must be at least ten percent less than the MEO to be judged a winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-year funding bids must be for a minimum of three years; for single-year funding, bids will cover two fiscal years after the initial year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-year review requirement for in-house activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial activities which remain in-house are required to have another review five years after the original study was conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic review ensures continued evaluation of conversion potential and cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thresholds and process for returning a contracted activity to in-house
rubrics_metrics.description: To return an activity to in-house performance, the new MEO must demonstrate performing in-house would be ten percent cheaper than the cost charged by the commercial source plus 25% of the commercial source's capital assets cost. Practically, this can require a government cost figure at least 20% cheaper than the original MEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval authority for returning an activity to in‑house rests with the Secretary or Director of the department or agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four implementation phases for conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of A-76 for existing or new services consists of four phases: inventory, management review, cost comparison, and implementation of cost comparison results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phases contain different steps depending on whether the service is existing or a new requirement; follow the specific step checklists for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision criteria checklist for existing services (13 steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table I steps/decision criteria for existing services: (1) Is activity a Governmental function? (2) Is function scheduled for inventory? (3) Is function scheduled for review? (4) Is in-house performance required for national defense? (5) Is in-house performance at a government hospital required by agency medical director? (6) Are satisfactory commercial sources available? (7) Would unacceptable delay occur? (8) Will contract be awarded under a Preferential Procurement Program? (9) Are less than ten FTEs present? (10) Does the Assistant Secretary waive the cost comparison? (11) Will the contract cost be unreasonable? (12) Conduct the cost comparison. (13) Is the contract cost less than in-house cost by the specified margin?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If activity is a governmental function, it is ineligible for conversion and review stops; activities with less than 10 FTEs should be considered for conversion if costs are reasonable. [Ref. 5:p.A-1]

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory grouping by FTE
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventory of commercial activities involves separating activities into two groups: those with 10 or fewer FTE work years and those with more than 10 FTEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One FTE is roughly equivalent to one employee; special procedures and considerations apply to small (≤10 FTE) activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management review considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Management review examines reasons that would preclude performance by a commercial source, including disruption/delay to DOD programs, requirements for training/readiness, absence of satisfactory commercial sources, availability from other federal agencies, or when contract performance is more costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps include assessing national defense requirements, agency medical director mandates, unacceptable delay, PPP applicability, and reviewing FTE counts; results determine whether to proceed to cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost comparison phase requirements and PWS importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost comparison begins with development of the Performance Work Statement and task analysis to identify and quantify output; concurrently prepare MEO and in-house cost estimate; compare MEO costs to commercial bids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS must be the most accurate and flawless piece of work in the study to obtain true equal-work cost estimates; the decision to award is based on whether contract costs are less than in-house costs by the specified margin (typically 10%).

rubrics_metrics.name: New services decision criteria and award thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Process for new requirements uses an 8-step checklist similar to existing services (Is activity governmental? national defense/hospital requirements? satisfactory commercial source? PPP? reasonableness of contract costs?) and awards contract if total contract costs are less than total in-house estimates by 10% of personnel costs and less than 25% of acquisition costs of equipment and plant necessary to perform the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is not reasonable to award a competitive contract without a cost comparison, conduct a cost comparison and apply the specified percentage thresholds. [Ref. 5:p.A-1]

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferential Procurement Program (PPP) handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If the activity will be awarded under a certain Preferential Procurement Program, no comparison of commercial and government costs is necessary and contracts are issued under the procuring agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Federal Prison Industries, handicapped industries, and other small and minority-owned firms; PPP exemption short-circuits standard A-76 comparison steps.
